excerpt: Reverse engineering the Nikon Z 6II with LLMs Two weeks back I posted about running Doom on the Nikon Z 6II, where I also introduced the qemu-expeed emulator I built. Today I want to talk a bit about how this went, and how this has made me feel about using LLMs in the reverse engineering process. For decorative purposes, I inserted some pictures I shot with my Z 6II and the Z 24-200 in summer 2025. Let me preface this by saying I don’t do this kind of thing professionally. By education I’m a mechanical engineer and by day I work on robotics software, with fancy filtering and control algorithms and quite a bit of math, which is on a far higher abstraction level than this project. In fact, this project was the first time I read assembly. Apart from general software skills, like knowing my way around Linux and Docker, probably most helpful was my bachelor’s in electrical engineering, which included a very decent course in chip design. (I’m grateful my alma mater allowed following a mechanical master after an electrical bachelor.) Like just about any other software engineer these days, I’ve been using LLMs (often called “GenAI” or even just plain “AI”) at work, and I noticed they were quite decent at getting things to “work” (more on those quotation marks later). That made me wonder whether they could be of help in getting some insight into my Nikon camera. Camera hacking has a long history, with Magic Lantern by far the most successful project. Originating around 2010 and the Canon EOS 5D Mark II, it has since spread to many Canon cameras and adds very relevant features like waveforms and raw video. Progress on Nikon cameras has been significantly more limited, however, and while Simeon Pilgrim and others of nikonhacker.com clearly put significant effort in this subject, their extensions were mostly limited to enabling and disabling existing features, and their project kind of fizzled out.
